one_liner: Managed C# 2D vector drawing on ImageSharp with a band-parallel CPU rasterizer and an optional WebGPU backend; the vendor reports 2.4x faster than single-threaded SkiaSharp 2.88.
what_it_does: ImageSharp.Drawing fills and strokes paths, polygons and SVG path data, and draws text through SixLabors.Fonts. It has solid, pattern, image and gradient brushes, dashed pens, clipping, layers, blend modes and image-processor masks. Everything goes through one DrawingCanvas API, into an ImageSharp Image<TPixel> (image.Mutate(c => c.Paint(canvas => ...))) or into WebGPU windows and offscreen render targets via the separate SixLabors.ImageSharp.Drawing.WebGPU package. canvas.CreateScene() records a retained scene that can be replayed with RenderScene. It is its own object model, not a SkiaSharp or System.Drawing drop-in.
how_it_is_fast: The CPU backend is a flush executor, not a command-at-a-time painter. A batch of drawing commands becomes a retained, row-oriented plan (FlushScene), built in parallel over contiguous command partitions. Paths are flattened once per (path, scale) and cached on the IPath, with rotation and translation carried as a residual matrix. Execution runs a Parallel.For over 16-pixel row bands with worker-local scratch. Each band uses a Blaze-derived 24.8 fixed-point area/cover scan converter (DEFAULT_RASTERIZER.md credits aurimasg/blaze) with bit-vector sparse cell tracking and precomputed start-cover seeds for winding entering from the left. Retained scenes keep the band-local line data and row plan, so a replay skips geometry work entirely. The WebGPU backend is a Vello-derived staged compute pipeline: path-tag prefix scans, binning, tile allocation, coarse and fine passes, with GPU bump-allocated scratch that grows on retry.
when_to_use: .NET services or tools already using ImageSharp that render large fill-heavy vector scenes (maps, charts, SVG-like content) to bitmaps, where one render may use every core.
Static or slowly changing scenes rendered many times (map tiles at a fixed zoom, dashboards): the retained-scene path took FillParis from 43.0 ms to 11.9 ms in the vendor's run.

Managed-only deployments: the CPU backend needs no native library, unlike SkiaSharp, whose Linux use needs a separate native-assets package (the benchmark project adds SkiaSharp.NativeAssets.Linux.NoDependencies).
.NET apps that want GPU drawing into WebGPU windows or offscreen targets with the same canvas code as the CPU path.
Drawing shaped, bidirectional or complex-script text into images through SixLabors.Fonts.
when_not_to_use: C or C++ code: this is a .NET library. Blend2D, Skia or Blaze are the native options.

Throughput per core, or many images rendered concurrently: the 2.4x CPU win sets every hardware thread against single-threaded SkiaSharp, and FillParis publishes no single-threaded ImageSharp row. FillTiger has an ImageSharp_SingleThreaded benchmark, but no published result was found.
Judging against current Skia: the benchmarks pin SkiaSharp 2.88.9 (at the v3.0.0 and v3.1.0 tags and on main), an older line than the SkiaSharp 4.150.1 pinned by the sister Fonts repo.

Untrusted SVG path data or geometry without limits: crashes on malformed SVG path input (#385, labelled security) and a StackOverflow in DefaultRasterizer.AddContainedLineF24Dot8 (#403) were fixed only in 2026.
Companies with 1M USD or more annual revenue using it directly in closed-source software, unless they buy the Six Labors commercial license.

integration.form: NuGet packages: SixLabors.ImageSharp.Drawing (managed) plus optional SixLabors.ImageSharp.Drawing.WebGPU (managed with per-RID native WebGPU runtime under runtimes/)
integration.dependencies: SixLabors.ImageSharp (>= 4.1.0 for 3.1.0, >= 4.1.2 for 3.1.1+), SixLabors.Fonts (>= 3.1.0), SixLabors.PolygonClipper (>= 1.0.1); WebGPU package adds Silk.NET.Windowing.Glfw and Silk.NET.Windowing.Sdl 2.23.0 (1.0.0 also used Silk.NET.WebGPU.Native.WGPU)
integration.min_toolchain: .NET 8 for the released 3.1.x packages (net8.0 asset); main was retargeted to net10.0/net11.0 (PR #416), and the README says the core package targets .NET 10
integration.platforms: CPU backend: any .NET platform (managed code). WebGPU backend: a GPU with WebGPU compute support and a bundled native library for the runtime identifier; WebGPUEnvironment probes compute-pipeline support at run time
integration.thread_safety: The rasterizer is static and keeps all mutable state in worker-owned scratch, and the CPU backend parallelizes internally. DrawingCanvas thread safety is not documented. DrawingTextCache became thread safe only with PR #420 (2026-09-14, after 3.1.0).

gotchas: The CPU backend fans out across all cores by default (Parallel.For over row bands, with partitions capped at Environment.ProcessorCount). Cap it with Configuration.MaxDegreeOfParallelism, as FillTiger's single-threaded variant does, when rendering many images concurrently.

Immediate mode is partly retained: Path and ComplexPolygon cache their flattened LinearGeometry per scale, so redrawing the same IPath objects skips curve subdivision. FillParis reuses one IPath list every iteration (its SVG has 79,353 relative cubic commands), while SkiaSharp rebuilds edges from each SKPath on every draw.

WebGPU flushes do not wait for the GPU. Scratch-overflow status is read back later (up to 8 pending flushes before a blocking resolve), and offscreen overflows are repaired by a corrective re-render, so call ReadbackImage when you need finished pixels. Timings of WebGPU flushes measure pipelined submission, not per-frame latency.

The released 3.1.x CPU rasterizer had small edge-accuracy errors, fixed on main by PR #417 (2026-09-11): band-boundary X drift of up to a few hundredths of a pixel on long slanted edges, coverage quantized to 1/256 before blending, and DDA walkers that floored rather than rounded.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Its CPU rasterizer is derived from Blaze and its GPU pipeline from Vello, so the reason to pick it is the platform: in .NET it gives you those designs plus a full 2D API (strokes, gradients, text, clipping, layers), which fill-only Blaze lacks. In C or C++, pick Blend2D (maintained, with its own multi-threaded context) or Blaze for fill throughput. In Rust, pick Vello CPU.
verified_claims_summary: The numbers come from the vendor's 3.1.0 release post, known only from search snippets because sixlabors.com is blocked. FillParis is the repo's paris-30k.svg: 50,620 path elements counted in the 14.0 MB file, a 1096x1060 map, fill-only with opacity. It ran on an AMD Ryzen AI Max+ 395 with Radeon 8060S under Windows 11 and .NET 10, using BenchmarkDotNet with Server GC (0.15.8 is pinned at v3.1.0). Results: SkiaSharp 103.4 ms, System.Drawing 147.3 ms, ImageSharp CPU 43.0 ms (2.4x), CPU retained 11.9 ms (8.7x), WebGPU 20.0 ms (5.2x), WebGPU retained 5.6 ms (18.5x); ratios are derived from page data. The baseline is SkiaSharp 2.88.9 drawing single-threaded into a CPU raster SKSurface, while ImageSharp uses every hardware thread, reuses cached flattened curves even in the immediate row, and in the WebGPU rows runs on the integrated GPU with non-blocking submits. No pixel comparison is made: VerifyOutput only saves PNGs.
